regions.power_system: PREPA owns the grid but no longer runs it: LUMA Energy has held the transmission-and-distribution O&M contract since June 2021, and Genera PR (a New Fortress Energy subsidiary) has run PREPA's legacy thermal generation fleet under a public-private O&M agreement since 2023, tasked to 'manage, operate, maintain and eventually decommission some of all the Legacy Generation Assets, base-load generation plants and peaking plants.' In the 12 months to April 2026 fossil fuels supplied about 97% of generation: natural gas 47%, coal about 17%, plus fuel oil, against solar 1.4% and wind 1.1%.
regions.price: US$0.26/kWh residential, effective 2026-01-01 (a $0.012739/kWh cut from the prior quarter's fuel and purchased-power adjustment)
regions.nuclear_position: No legal ban on nuclear power. Puerto Rico's legislature passed a 2018 law directing a study of nuclear feasibility for the island. A Puerto Rico House bill on nuclear-energy research was reported under committee review in January 2025.
regions.microreactor_activity: The Nuclear Alternative Project (NAP), a Puerto Rico-based nonprofit founded in 2016, obtained DOE Office of Nuclear Energy sponsorship for a Preliminary Feasibility Study for SMRs and microreactors, carried out via Idaho National Laboratory (findings released May 2020), which concluded advanced reactors 'can meet Puerto Rico's unique energy needs by complementing renewable sources with zero-emission electricity resilient to extreme natural events.' In 2021 DOE awarded NAP about $1.6 million for a site-suitability phase, which named two candidate sites, one lying 'on the island's north coast near an industrial hub' and the other 'on its east coast at the former Roosevelt Roads Naval Station' (a decommissioned base, not an active military installation). NAP also reported a commissioned survey of over 3,000 residents finding 94% interested in continuing to explore nuclear energy. No reactor vendor, NRC license application or in-service date had been announced as of this pass.
blockers: No reactor vendor selected and no NRC license application filed as of this pass
Generation is split between LUMA (transmission and distribution) and Genera (legacy thermal generation), so no single utility counterparty yet owns a nuclear procurement decision
2025-2026 regulatory attention is on emergency thermal procurement (Genera's request to acquire 700-850 MW of temporary generation) rather than nuclear
regions.microreactor_read: The DOE-funded feasibility case is the most advanced of any US island jurisdiction, with two named candidate sites and a favorable resident survey, but nobody has converted it into an RFP, an NRC docket or a signed PPA counterparty since 2021 — the buyer-side vacuum, not the technical case, is what is missing.

regions.power_system: WAPA (Virgin Islands Water and Power Authority) runs two separate island grids on delivered fuel: St. Thomas/St. John and St. Croix, with 238 MW of installed capacity as of 2020 (138 MW St. Thomas district, 100 MW St. Croix), historically burning a propane/diesel mix (74% propane, 26% diesel in March 2020). WAPA's Phase II Wartsila project — four new dual-fuel engines able to run on LPG or light fuel oil, rated at 36 MW and able to 'power 55% of the St. Thomas/St. John district' — reached completion at a ribbon-cutting on 2025-01-17.

loads.mw: 36 MW new capacity (within a 138 MW St. Thomas-district total, 2020 figure)

blockers: No named nuclear feasibility study, MOU or vendor interest to build on, unlike Puerto Rico
WAPA's 2023-2025 capital program is already committed to new propane-capable thermal units (Wartsila Phase II)
Two disconnected island grids (St. Thomas/St. John and St. Croix) mean a single unit serves only part of the territory's ~238 MW system
regions.microreactor_read: USVI pays a delivered-fuel retail price (42 cents/kWh) close to Puerto Rico's, but with zero feasibility work, MOUs or legislative interest on record, so a microreactor sale here starts years behind Puerto Rico rather than riding alongside it.

regions.power_system: Guam Power Authority (GPA) is the sole civilian utility; its oil-fired fleet has been joined by the new Ukudu power plant, which a Consolidated Commission on Utilities member said in November 2024 'can make power at 5 (cents) per kWh plus fuel at 11 cents to 13 cents per kWh' -- roughly 16-18 cents/kWh all-in, cheaper than the legacy oil-fired units it supplements.
regions.price: LEAC (fuel cost adjustment) proposed to fall from $0.208802/kWh to $0.188781/kWh effective 2025-08-01, then to $0.135840/kWh effective 2025-09-01 as Ukudu came online; the residential base rate was separately proposed to rise about 2.2-2.8 cents/kWh in the same filing
regions.nuclear_position: GPA operates no licensed reactor. A 2023 territorial bill, the 'Nuclear Energy Prohibition Act' (Bill 151-37, introduced by Sen. Sabina Flores Perez, Speaker Therese Terlaje and Sen. Chris Barnett), would add a new Guam Code chapter under which 'no nuclear fission power plant, small modular reactors or nuclear microreactors shall be constructed, imported or used, and no radioactive material shall be disposed of on Guam'; no enactment into public law was confirmed in this pass, and as of Nov 2024-Feb 2025 reporting it remained a live proposal under committee discussion. Guam's own Public Utilities Commission chairman argued against it, saying 'the Legislature should not prohibit fair and open considerations of all technologies.'
regions.microreactor_activity: Secondary reporting describes a 2012 GPA dialogue with NuScale Power on small modular reactors, not independently confirmed against a NuScale or GPA primary source in this pass. In November 2024 a Consolidated Commission on Utilities member cited small (1-3 MW) nuclear plant power costs of 47 cents/kWh against Ukudu's 16-18 cents/kWh all-in, concluding 'someday, nuclear can make sense. But not in the near future.'
blockers: A pending territorial bill would prohibit constructing, importing or using any nuclear fission plant, SMR or microreactor on Guam; final legislative status unconfirmed in this pass
GPA's own utility commissioner puts small-reactor power cost (47 cents/kWh) at roughly 3x the new Ukudu gas/diesel plant's all-in cost (16-18 cents/kWh)
Separate 2026-2027 NDAA activity concerns a Department of Defense SMR pilot for Indo-Pacific Command -- a defense track distinct from, and politically entangled with, GPA's civilian system
regions.microreactor_read: GPA's newest conventional plant already prices near 16-18 cents/kWh and the territory's own utility regulator cites 47 cents/kWh for small nuclear, so civilian Guam is not a near-term buyer until unit cost falls well below an already-improving oil-fired benchmark, and a pending territorial ban would have to be resolved first.

regions.power_system: The Commonwealth Utilities Corporation (CUC) runs diesel generation on Saipan, Tinian and Rota with 'near-total reliance on imported petroleum products for both electricity generation and transportation' and 'aging electricity infrastructure and vulnerability to natural disasters.' Saipan's plants (Power Plant 1 designed for 86 MW across eight units, Plant 2 at 10 MW, Plant 4 at 16 MW) were reported at 62.1 MW combined availability in March 2025; a 2026 typhoon cut that further, with a recovery update citing 42.5 MW restored on Saipan and Rota timelines still being set.
regions.price: US$0.19-0.33/kWh residential range, 2025 (DOE); CUC's own comparison put CNMI at US$0.2749/kWh residential in November 2024, called the lowest among US-affiliated Pacific jurisdictions versus $0.4139/kWh in Guam, $0.4414/kWh on Hawaii Island and $0.3986/kWh in American Samoa at that date. A separate Fuel Adjustment Charge of $0.21119/kWh took effect 2025-03-01; CUC's base rate has been unchanged since April 2014.

regions.nuclear_position: No CNMI nuclear ban found. Senator Jude Hofschneider pre-filed Senate Joint Resolution 24-05 supporting federal study, evaluation and possible future deployment of small modular reactors and microreactors on Saipan, Tinian or Rota, while the resolution itself concedes 'the CNMI does not have the financial capacity to independently fund the installation, operation, or long-term maintenance of such systems.' A CNMI House member has separately opposed nuclear technology in the territory in the context of the Department of Defense's Project JANUS, a distinct military proposal, per local reporting not independently fetched in this pass.
regions.microreactor_activity: SJR 24-05 is framed as civilian and federal-facing: it 'does not authorise construction of a nuclear facility' but 'calls for federal agencies to consider Saipan, Tinian and Rota for feasibility studies, pilot programmes or possible future deployment,' citing exposure to volatile imported-fuel prices and grid damage from a recent super typhoon. No funded federal study or agency response was found as of this pass.
blockers: SJR 24-05 was pre-filed/introduced but had not, as of this pass, produced a funded federal study or agency commitment
The resolution's own text states CNMI lacks the financial capacity to fund installation, operation or long-term maintenance of any such system
Civilian nuclear interest (SJR 24-05) sits alongside a separate, opposed military reactor proposal (Project JANUS), risking public conflation of the two
2026 typhoon damage has CUC focused on restoring diesel capacity on Saipan and Rota rather than evaluating new generation types
regions.microreactor_read: A sitting CNMI senator has already put Saipan, Tinian and Rota on record asking the federal government to study microreactors -- an unusually direct civilian ask among the territories -- but the same resolution admits CNMI cannot pay for one itself, so any deal has to be federally funded or vendor-financed, not locally procured, and has to be kept visibly separate from the contested military reactor proposal next to it.

regions.power_system: American Samoa Power Authority (ASPA) generates almost entirely on imported diesel -- diesel-dependent generation is about 97% of output, with solar about 11% of installed utility-scale capacity but only about 3% of generation (2023) -- and 'spends about $27 million to $30 million on diesel every year.' Construction began in 2024 on the first phase of a 20-megawatt Pavaiai solar PV project, and a 4-megawatt/8-megawatt-hour battery system was commissioned in early 2025.
regions.price: 43 cents/kWh average retail price, 2023 (about 3.5x the US average); ASPA states 'ASPA's cost for electric generation today is about 27-cents per kilowatt hour' (24 cents fuel, 3 cents O&M), projected to fall to about 11 cents/kWh once new solar and wind independent-power-producer contracts are online

regions.microreactor_activity: none found -- searched ASPA's own site and general microreactor literature for any American-Samoa-specific MOU, feasibility study or vendor visit. Any future outreach should be handled with care given the wider Pacific region's history with nuclear-weapons-test fallout, even though American Samoa itself was not a test site.
blockers: No nuclear feasibility study, MOU or legislative interest found to build on
ASPA's capital program is already committed to the Pavaiai solar (20 MW) and battery (4 MW/8 MWh) builds now under construction
The StarKist cannery feeder (27 MW peak) is close to the top of the 1-20 MW range alone, on a small isolated grid with limited other load to spread fixed reactor costs across
regions.microreactor_read: ASPA's diesel bill (about 27 cents/kWh, $27-30M/year in fuel alone) is exactly the delivered-fuel cost a reactor should beat, and the StarKist cannery's 27 MW peak shows the territory can host a load at microreactor scale -- but ASPA has already committed its near-term capital to solar-plus-storage (Pavaiai, and previously Ta'u) rather than nuclear, and no study has opened that door.
